AutoPerf.title: AutoPerf
AutoPerf.content:
Intro
AutoPerf is a tool that I built for automated performance testing of data distribution service.
Built entirely in Python all by myself.
How does it work?

Define configuration

What parameters do you want to vary
What values per parameter?

Do you have specific values you want to try?
Do you want to randomly sample values?


Do you have a specific list of experiments that you want to run?
What machines are you working with?

Which machines should have pubs/subs/both?


How many times should you run each experiment?
How many times should you retry an experiment if it fails?
Do you want to add simulated network noise?

random delays
packet loss
packet corruption




Run the experiment.

Ping machines to check their accessible
Restart all machines
Check accessibility
Launch experiment scripts per machine
Wait for experiment to end


Download data from each machine.
Run next experiment until end of campaign.

Challenges

sometimes machines are unreachable (both via ping or ssh)
when one machine fails, all others continue running anyway
experiments with no data
experiments with data from previously running experiments
experiments that fail on first try but eventually succeed when rerun

Mistakes

not using OOP at the start
not having an explicit config file - configuration settings were hardcoded into source code

Technical Decisions

choosing Python

easiest to write in
quick to write
lots of libraries from community to do what I needed

e.g. paramiko for SSH connection




not using OOP at the start

got really messy
eventually moved to OOP

real-life painful lesson of the benefits of OOP





What I’d Do Differently

Learn and write in Rust.
Use a database - maybe something like MongoDB because data is very tabular.

Future Work
How to scale?
How to optimise?

Data-Distribution-Service-(DDS).title: Data Distribution Service (DDS)
Data-Distribution-Service-(DDS).content:
middleware
used in real time mission critical systems e.g. air traffic control, autonomous vehicles, energy management systems, medical IoT
uses publish-subscribe paradigm

publishers send data on certain topics using data writers

data writers are entities contained in pubs that write messages on a specific single topic


subscribers receive data on certain topics using data readers

data readers are entities contained in subs that read messages on a specific topic




pubs and subs can be added in real-time

Dotfiles.title: Dotfiles
Dotfiles.content:
You can find my dotfiles here. Here are the main applications that I’ve configured in my dotfiles:

aerospace
Neovim
sketchybar
Tmux
Visidata
Zsh

Aerospace
Aerospace is a window tiling manager that I use on Mac. It lets you control all windows, their sizing, their layout (including horizontal and vertical splits), which monitors to show them on, and even when to show them, using the keyboard.
NeoVim
My editor of choice. Super highly configurable and I’ve configured it just the way I like. The biggest improvement I can remember is adding neotest to let you run tests and see their outcomes while you stay in the code. It saves you having a dedicated tmux pane for running unit tests.
SketchyBar
A custom application toolbar on Mac that I’ve customised to show Aerospace windows too. It shows the exact icons and outputs of commands (like checking the network download and upload throughput) that I choose.
Tmux
An application for terminal multiplexing. I’ve set up my custom keybinds for splitting panes, creating windows, and even switching between sessions.
visidata
A tool I use for viewing and manipulating tabular data. It uses vim motions which makes it easy to navigate the data. I’ve even created and used my own custom plugins e.g. I created a plugin to calculate the mean with 95% confidence interval for any column of data.
zsh
My shell of choice.

Evaluating-the-Performance-of-Data-Distr.title: Evaluating the Performance of Data Distribution Service using Statistical Methods
Evaluating-the-Performance-of-Data-Distr.content:
Problem:

need to evaluate performance of DDS to better understand it
not easy to get performance of expensive configurations
the longer you run the performance test the better
too many configurations to look at


typically people evaluate a specific scenario
can we collect a lot of data and use Statistical Methods to analyse it?
can we look at how specific parameters impact the performance?
can we look at how interactions between parameters affect the performance?

Context:


DDS used publish-subscribe


you have pubs that send data on a topic


subs received data on a topic


pubs and subs can be added and removed in real-time


there are 2 types of parameters for configuring communication

qos

defined in the DDS spec
reliability:

reliable: wait for ack before sending next message
best effort: just send. Don’t care about ack


durability:

0: don’t send or store previously sent messages
1: send previously sent messages to new subs
2: use main memory to store previously sent messages and resend to new subs
3: use secondary memory to store previously sent messages and resend to new subs




non-qos

general parameters not specified in DDS spec but still generally applicable to networks
data lenth: size of messages
multicast:

unicast: send 1 messages n times to n subs
multicast: send n messages 1 time to n subs


sub count
pub count





solution

run performance tests on various configurations for different parameters values
gather lots of data
analyse the data

isolate specific parameters

compare their values using ecdfs
find most performant value


analyse which paramter values often are most performant
analyse interactions with other parameter values

which combinations of parameters are more performant than others?

How-I-Got-to-130WPM-Typing-Speed.filePath: How I Got to 130WPM Typing Speed.md
How-I-Got-to-130WPM-Typing-Speed.title: How I Got to 130WPM Typing Speed
How-I-Got-to-130WPM-Typing-Speed.content:
That is a screenshot of my fastest typing speed recorded on my MonkeyType profile. That is a speed of 131 words per minute (WPM). But its just a single data point…and with my background, I appreciate distributions and the nature of being statistical, so below is my entire distribution of typing speeds.

My distribution of typing speeds as recorded via MonkeyType before and after practicing on keybr.
For context, according to Wikipedia, “professional typists type at speeds of 43 to 80 wpm”. Table 1 of this paper shows an average WPM of 65 and 87 for 2 separate studies looking at typing speeds. It’s safe to say that my typing speed is above the average typist.
Is it really though?
…
I don’t think so.
MonkeyType tests your typing speed with the most common and easy to type words which means the typing speed measured is likely inflated. Below, is my top typing speed according to keybr, a total of 128 WPM and beats 99.84% of all other people (at least other people being keybr’s other users). Why is keybr’s WPM a better measure than MonkeyType? Because it tests you on any English word and therefore more similarly replicates the paper mentioned. So, how did I get here?

My top typing speed according to keybr is 127.6wpm and beats 99.84% of all other people.
It started many years ago. I was in my early teens, I think 13 or 14, and I wanted to be a cool hacker. The type you would see in movies who could type real fast on a keyboard and hack into the system mainframe in seconds. So I wanted to learn how to type fast and after browing a few Reddit posts I came across the concept of touch typing. Up to that point, I, and most people, type by pecking at the keyboard with 1 or 2 fingers and we got quite good at it which did make us faster…but it could be even faster. Touch typing introduces the concept of using all 8 fingers (not counting thumbs of course) to type instead of just 1 or 2.
There are now many free websites out there that help teach you how to touch type by giving you typing drills. These systems enforce the use of all fingers for specific fingers which build up your muscle memory. The one I use these days is keybr.com. It’ll start you off with (what seems like) random combinations of letters which get you more comfortable with the finger placements. After a lot of practice you can then move on to words. I personally use keybr with words and here is the daily routine I use to practice my typing to improve it.
I start by “warming up” with some MonkeyType 30-second tests. I usually do about 3. The first is just a warm up, the second is where I slow down and aim to get 100%, and the third is where I speed up while keeping accuracy as high as I can. After these 3 runs I then start on keybr. I do a typing test on keybr and then practice and then do another typing test on keybr after the practice. I make sure to do at least 10 minutes of keybr everyday.
The question is…why do all this work? Is it really worth it to type faster? Does it actually improve your typing speed? Here is a graph showing various stats from my typing lessons over time. Purple is the number of keys per lesson, orange/brown is my accuracy and green is my typing speed.

Horizontal axis: lesson number. Vertical axis: typing speed (green), accuracy (orange/brown), number of keys in lesson (purple).
Take a good look at it.
Seriously. Go back and look.
What do you notice?
Here is what I notice. The graph can be split horizontally into a left side and right side around the 700th lesson where the green and brown “lines” cross over.
On the left, my speed was higher but my accuracy was lower which tells us that if I prioritise speed over accuracy I am much more inaccurate. One noticeable thing from the graph is how the gap between speed and accuracy increases before the switching point. Yes, the green points rise quite high, BUT, the orange points sink lower…
On the other hand, on the right side, both the typing speed in green and the accuracy in orange/brown slowly increase over the lessons over time and this signifies that my speed will get faster over time if I continue to prioritise accuracy.
So this system does work. Doing 15 minutes of typing practice a day (10 minutes practice + typing tests) everyday improves both your speed and accuracy - at least in my case. Of course, this assumes you prioritise accuracy over speed when you are practicing. Over the months and after reading many Reddit posts and various articles, I have configured my keybr settings to maximise typing improvement/learning. Here is a breakdown of the settings that are not the default and why:
Target Typing Speed: 100wpm + “unlock next key only when the previous keys are also above the target speed”
I aim to type more than 100wpm so I set the target typing speed at 100wpm. This means that keybr does not proceed to the next letter until I hit 100wpm which forces you to drill a specific letter. In most cases, you drill it enough and it reaches 100wpm. Funnily enough, I’ve noticed that keybr sometimes does not stricly enforce this. I’ve noticed cases where it proceeds to another letter despite being under 100wpm. Nonetheless, the variation ensures that I don’t get rusty on letters that I haven’t worked on in a while.
Prefer Natural Words
I have reached a point where I am comfortable with the finger placements and touch typing technique and can therefore practice using natural words as the whole point of learning to type faster is to type - which usually involves typing natural words…
Repeat Each Word: 2
By repeating each word twice, I reinforce the muscle memory because I am typing the word again, regardless of if I typed it incorrectly or not on the first instance of the word. This is especially good in the case where you make a mistake in the first instance of the word because you get a second chance to retype the word correctly which further reinforces the correct muscle memory.
Add Words to Lessons: About 40%
In my experimentation, I found this to be the sweet spot of number of words where it was long enough to aim for 100% accuracy but short enough to forgive inaccuracies. What does that mean? When I tried longer lessons, I found myself more likely to make at least one mistake and when lessons were shorter I found the opposite, I was more likely to make no mistakes. 40% was a good balance to challenge me to aim for 100% accuracy but long enough where I had a chance of making mistakes. I found that this boundary was the perfect zone for challenging myself accuracy-wise.
That concludes my daily typing practice to boost my typing speed up to ~130WPM. 3 warm up runs with MonkeyType. 1 test, 10 minutes practice, and another test on keybr. Do this consistently and you may see results like with me. Just remember, it’s always hardest in the beginning. It’ll get easier over time - just stick to it. You got this!

How-I-Read-Papers.title: How I Read Papers
How-I-Read-Papers.content:
When I first started my PhD I had no idea how to actually read a paper. I would spend hours reading and re-reading papers and making notes and trying to highlight main points and trying to draw the main contributions from a paper. Some of these papers that I would spend hours reading and understanding were sometimes vaguely of not relevant to my work. I realised (just like in other areas of my work and life) my current system was not the best.
I use the 3 pass method from How to Read a Paper. In it’s essence you do the following 3 passes where each pass builds upon the last:

Pass 1

5 to 10 mins
read the

title
abstract
intro
headings and subheadings
conclusion




Pass 2

up to 1 hour
rest the entire paper while skipping details like proofs and algorithms


Pass 3

up to 6 hours
virtually recreate the paper



Pass 1
⏱ 5 to 10 minutes
Read the title, abstract, intro, headings + subheadings, and conclusion.
At the end of the first pass you have a vague idea of what the paper is about.
I usually aim to answer the following questions after pass 1:

Category: What kind of paper is this? Novel system? Evaluation of existing methods? Etc.
Clarity: Was it easy to read?
Context: What existing methods/techniques did this paper use?
Contributions: What are the main contributions of this paper?
Correctness: Are the mentioned assumptions valid?

With this info you can decide whether its worth reading further or to be discarded. If good to continue reading then you do pass 2.
Pass 2
⏱ up to 1 hour
This is the point where you read the entire paper from start to finish. Ignore the details e.g. proofs and algorithms. Write notes. Make annotations. Write comments. Question things.
At the end of pass 2 you should be able to summarise the work to a colleague.
Pass 3
⏱ up to 6 hours…
This pass takes the longest because you will be virtually recreating the work. You present yourself wth the same problem, same context, and the same assumptions, and then you basically create your own solution as if you were doing the work of the paper before the paper was written.
Find and challenge every assumption.
Write down ideas for future work.
You then compare your recreation with the paper.
At the end of this pass you shoud be able to:

recreate the entire paper from memory
find strengths and weaknesses of the paper
find hidden assumptions
find missing citations to relevant work
find potential issues with experiments or analytical techniques

And that is how I read papers using 3 passes. I hope you learnt something new today - if not, feel free to share how you read papers. You can email me at mail@KaleemPeeroo.com.

How-I-Remember-What-I-Read.filePath: How I Remember What I Read.md
How-I-Remember-What-I-Read.title: How I Remember What I Read
How-I-Remember-What-I-Read.content:
For a long time I would read non-fiction books and a few months later I would remember maybe 2 or 3 things from what I read. It seemed like a waste of time. All that time spent reading and not remembering everything I wanted to remember. That system was not working. I couldn’t rely on my brain to absorb and store 100% of what I read. Even 50% of what I read. I had to come up with a new system.
I searched for the most effective methods to remember things and found 2 keys things: flash cards and spaced repetition. These were the fundamental blocks for my new system. I’ve used flash cards and spaced repetition before, during my undergrad to study various computer science topics. It worked well back then so I assumed it would work well now. So I wanted to find a way to create this new system.
My current system for reading at the time would let me highlight content from books which would be stored in Obsidian. I’d then write my own notes of my highlights. Now all I had to do is create flash cards and use spaced repetition. Back in undergrad, I used Anki for that. Luckily Obsidian has a plugin called spaced repetition which lets you create flashcards within your notes and use spaced repetition to schedule when to review them. You even have the option to hide content in your notes using closures to act as flash cards. So I started using it which meant going through my notes and creating flash cards from them which took some time.
I broke it down and created a task in my daily note template to add or improve at least 1 flash card a day. It’s the same system I’ve used to write blog posts or do anything big - I just do a little chunk everyday. In the case of writing blog posts I have a task to write at least 1 sentence a day. Including this post that you’re reading right now. Chances are this sentence was written on a different day as the first sentence of this post. In fact, this very sentence that you are reading at the moment was written the day after the previous sentence. This system lets me slowly add flash cards day after day. The great thing about spaced repetition is that over time I review less and less cards.
I reached a point where I had managed to successfully create flashcards from my existing content. Everyday I would spend 5 to 10 minutes reviewing flashcards. That’s the key to this whole system. You. Reviewing flashcards. Everyday. It’s the little thing that you do everyday that compounds over time. You review the flashcards for a few minutes everyday and after months you’ll be remembering facts like you’re taking that miracle drug from the movie Limitless.
As time goes on I would read new books, annotate them and then create flash cards for the annotations in Obsidian. To this day, I continue reading, annotating, creating flash cards, and reviewing them every day and it works really well for me. So I want to share this with the world and that’s why I created ReadToRetain.
ReadToRetain is my system available for you. You just paste in your notes and it’ll generate flash cards for you that you can review daily. It’s a proven way to memorise what you read/study.
If you’re interested in trying it out let me know how you get along. Send me a message at mail@kaleempeeroo.com.

How-I-transitioned-to-Vim.title: How I transitioned to Vim
How-I-transitioned-to-Vim.content:
This is the story of how I transitioned to VIM in the hope that it helps you transition to VIM too.
When I first started coding I used good ol’ Sublime text. Then in 2018, I moved to good ol’ Visual Studio Code and never looked back. I actually looked forward. Forward to VIM which has many benefits though I won’t list them here to save us both time.
The problem was that the transition to VIM was a big step…and big first steps are always hard. I started by enabling VIM mode in VSC. I watched tutorials and learned the basics through vimtutor and then forced myself to continue writing code using VIM mode in VSC. I’m not going to lie…it was hard in the beginning. Fighting the urge to go back to the ol’ ways of navigating code was a recurring thing. I remember getting fat fingers during a meeting while showing some code to a supervisor. My cursor was going everywhere but where I wanted it to go. The pressure was exaggerating the learning curve. Eventually you get used to the movements and you form the muscle memory. You feel less and less friction over time until you come to the realisation that it’s time to move to VIM, the application.
That’s when I decided to use Neovim but I didn’t know where to start and which config to use. There were so many options. After browsing a few Reddit posts and talking to a friend who used Neovim I ended up picking LazyVim. I think of myself as lazy. Others may call it efficient. Maybe that’s why I chose LazyVim. Regardless, it was nice. I was surprised at how well the application mimicked an IDE like VSC. You could browse files, create panes for terminal usage, see debug output, etc. It was nice. For a while. There were so many plugins and I didn’t know what each plugin did. It took too much time going through each plugin, learning what it does, how it works, and how to configure it.
So, I decided to do what probably every NeoVim user has done numerous times. I redid my config. I removed everything related to LazyVim and just created a single config file. I only added the plugins that I understood and wanted to use. One of the first ones I added was Oil. Oil lets you treat your filesystem as if it were a vim buffer. As if your list of files was the content of a text file which lets you copy paste lines (files), delete them, and the other useful file system stuff like navigation and renaming.
That was also the time when I discovered Language Server Protocols (LSPs) which blew my mind. I love finding out how things work and looking behind the scenes at things and I found out that LSPs are a big part of IDEs like VSC. Proof that using nvim indirectly teaches you about what’s happening under the hood which strengthens your overall systems knowledge. I installed a plugin called mason.nvim which made it so easy to install LSPs and highly recommend it to anyone using nvim. As I added more and more plugins that I understood and appreciated, my config file became longer and longer. At the time my config was all just a single file. It got messy. Very long and messy.
So, I decided to do what probably every NeoVim user has done numerous times. I redid my config. I split the file up into a plugins folder and put each plugin into its own single file. This meant it was a lot easier to find the plugin and reconfigure it when I had to. To this day it’s remained like this and I think it’s the best way to organise your Neovim plugins.
So what have I learnt and what could you learn? Start learning vim motions by enabling vim mode in your IDE. Also try out vimtutor, an application that’s installed with vim. Once you’re familiar with the motions you can move to NeoVim. I’d recommend starting with no plugins and adding them one by one.
Over time you’ll have a custom list of plugins that are specific for you and great for you. I think that’s the best part, Neovim evolves into the best tool for you. You just have to invest into it. I have, and I believe that my investment has paid off.

MY-ARXIV-2023-Publication-on-Data-Availa.filePath: MY ARXIV 2023 Publication on Data Availability Sampling.md
MY-ARXIV-2023-Publication-on-Data-Availa.title: MY ARXIV 2023 Publication on Data Availability Sampling
MY-ARXIV-2023-Publication-on-Data-Availa.content:
ARXIV 2023: Data Availability Sampling in Ethereum: Analysis of P2P Networking Requirements

Abstract
Despite their increasing popularity, blockchains still suffer from severe scalability limitations. Recently, Ethereum proposed a novel approach to block validation based on Data Availability Sampling (DAS), that has the potential to improve its transaction per second rate by more than two orders of magnitude. DAS should also significantly reduce per-transaction validation costs. At the same time, DAS introduces new communication patterns in the Ethereum Peer-to-Peer (P2P) network. These drastically increase the amount of exchanged data and impose stringent latency objectives. In this paper, we review the new requirements for P2P networking associated with DAS, discuss open challenges, and identify new research directions.

MY-ARXIV-2023-Publication-on-Data-Distri.filePath: MY ARXIV 2023 Publication on Data Distribution Service.md
MY-ARXIV-2023-Publication-on-Data-Distri.title: MY ARXIV 2023 Publication on Data Distribution Service
MY-ARXIV-2023-Publication-on-Data-Distri.content:
ARXIV 2023: A Survey on Experimental Performance Evaluation of Data Distribution Service (DDS) Implementations

Abstract
The Data Distribution Service (DDS) is a widely used communication specification for real-time mission-critical systems that follow the principles of publish-subscribe middleware. DDS has an extensive set of quality of service (QoS) parameters allowing a thorough customisation of the intended communication. An extensive survey of the performance of the implementations of this communication middleware is lacking. This paper closes the gap by surveying the state of the art in performance of various DDS implementations and identifying any research gaps that exist within this domain.

MY-CGVC-2024-Publication.title: MY CGVC 2024 Publication
MY-CGVC-2024-Publication.content:
CGVC 2024: Best Poster Winner: Visualising the Impact of High-dimensional Configuration Parameters on the Performance of Data Distribution Service

Abstract
Data Distribution Service (DDS) is a specification for middleware in real-time and mission-critical systems such as energy management systems and medical devices. Such systems have specific performance requirements to function properly and avoid catastrophe. However, the performance of the system can vary depending on the various parameters defined before or during run-time. Understanding how the different parameters impact performance helps DDS system designers set up distributed systems in critical domains. This work introduces a workflow for understanding how parameter values can affect system performance, as seen in their distribution form. It applies to DDS and any configurable system with multiple parameters that can take multiple values that may result in different system performance. This visualisation workflow is demonstrated on a dataset created by running tests on an actual DDS system. We argue that they help understand non-linear relationships between the parameters and DDS performance and help identify anomalous results that may need investigation.

MY-EDCC-2022-Publication.title: MY EDCC 2022 Publication
MY-EDCC-2022-Publication.content:
EDCC 2022: Exploring the Effects of Multicast Communication on DDS Performance

Abstract
The Data Distribution Service (DDS) is an Object Management Group (OMG) standard for high-performance and real-time systems. DDS is a data-centric middleware based on the publish-subscribe communication pattern and is used in many mission-critical, or even safety-critical, systems such as air traffic control and robot operating system (ROS2).
This research aims at identifying how the usage of multicast affects the performance of DDS communication for varying numbers of participants (publishers and subscribers). The results show that DDS configured for multicast communication can exhibit worse performance under a high load (a greater number of participants) than DDS configured for unicast communication. This counter-intuitive result reinforces the need for researchers and practitioners to be clear about the details of how multicast communication operates on the network.

MY-EDCC-2024-Publication.title: MY EDCC 2024 Publication
MY-EDCC-2024-Publication.content:
EDCC 2024: Machine Learning for Performance Prediction of Data Distribution Service (DDS) Paper

Abstract
Networking middleware following the Data Distribution Service (DDS) specification is used in real-time mission-critical systems such as autonomous vehicles, energy management systems, and air traffic control. DDS follows the publish-subscribe communication pattern and offers a set of Quality of Service (QoS) parameters, allowing the users to align the data communication to the needs of the application.Configuring DDS to achieve the required performance is a difficult task, given the large space of QoS parameter values. Experimental evaluation of performance levels with a real DDS system for different QoS configurations can be complex and require substantial time and resources.We propose the use of Machine Learning (ML) models to predict the performance metric distribution of DDS under different configurations. This is done by using performance measurements of some configurations to train an ML model. The trained model can then be used to predict the performance distribution of DDS under other system configurations. Since the prediction is computationally inexpensive, we can predict the performance of many different configurations to find a suitable one for given requirements. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time this approach has been applied to DDS performance evaluation.We used random forests (RF) as an ML method and linear regression (LR) as a baseline. We selected thirteen performance metrics, and for each, we trained an RF model and tuned its hyperparameters. We tested the final models on system configurations unseen during training, both for parameter values within the training range (interpolation) and outside the training range (extrapolation).The RF models show better predictive accuracy than the LR baseline. This paper focuses on the models for throughput and latency - the two well-established performance metrics. The models demonstrate coefficients of determination greater than 0.9 and 0.8, respectively, for different unseen system configurations in interpolation, but work less well in extrapolation cases.We conclude that the proposed ML models offer a way of predicting the performance distribution of a range of configurations when interpolation is used. Since model prediction is computationally much cheaper than relying on experimentation, it is a useful tool to guide DDS system parametrisation and design.

My-MIDDLEWARE-2025-Publication.title: My MIDDLEWARE 2025 Publication
My-MIDDLEWARE-2025-Publication.content:
MIDDLEWARE 2025: PANDAS: Peer-to-peer, Adaptive Networking Allowing Data Availability Sampling within Ethereum Consensus Timebounds

Abstract
Layer-2 protocols such as rollups can help address Ethereum’s throughput limits. An efficient data availability layer is key for layer-2 support in Ethereum, but broadcast methods do not scale. A promising approach is the selective distribution of layer-2 data and its verification by data availability sampling (DAS). Integrating DAS with Ethereum consensus is, however, a challenge, as data must be shared and sampled within 4 seconds of each consensus slot.
We propose PANDAS, a practical approach to integrating DAS with Ethereum without modifying Ethereum’s core protocols. PANDAS disseminates layer-2 data and samples its availability using lightweight, direct exchanges. Its design accounts for message loss, node failures, and unresponsive participants. Our evaluation in a 1,000-node cluster and simulations for up to 20,000 peers show that PANDAS allows layer-2 data dissemination and sampling under planetary-scale latencies within the 4-second deadline.

My-Principles-for-Weight-Training.title: My Principles for Weight Training
My-Principles-for-Weight-Training.content:
strength: move weight
Hypertrophy: move muscle
strength: 3 to 5 reps
hypertrophy: 5 to 15 reps
intensity is second most important thing (aim for 8 to 10 - I like the feeling of fighting the failure and pushing past your mental limit)
most important thing is moving the muscle - focus and get that mind-muscle connection

Predicting-the-Performance-of-Data-Distr.title: Predicting the Performance of Data Distribution Service via Percentile Regression using Machine Learning
Predicting-the-Performance-of-Data-Distr.content:
Data Distribution Service (DDS) system designers do not know how their systems will perform unless they run performance experiments that capture the desired behaviour. These performance experiments can be quite costly in terms of money, time, and power consumption. If one desires good enough performance (let alone optimal) for a system that operates within the constrains of its environment, then one must carry out many performance experiments for different system configurations. The costs increase depending on the configuration because larger systems with more publishers/subscribers and larger data lengths will likely take longer to record performance metrics compared to smaller systems with less publishers/subscribers and smaller data lengths. The problem, clearly defined, is that it costs time, money, and power consumption to find the most ideal performing configuration for a DDS system.
To the best of my knowledge, prior to my first publication on applying ML to Data Distribution Service (DDS), no literature was shown to solve this problem using this solution. In fact, no literature existed that solved the problem for distribuetd systems, let alone publish-subscribe middleware in general.

abstract

problem

people have to set up DDS systems
their scenarios may contain parameter choices e.g. X scenario can only use 7 pubs and 3 subs and send 100B of data

what about other parameters values?
which values would lead to best performance?
can’t know until you try

meaning you have to set up the system then run performance test
most of the time this is expensive, especially for bigger and more expensive configurations






others’ solutions

no one has predicted DDS performance yet


my solution

gather data
transform data into 23 percentiles to recreate distribution
train model to predict 23 percentiles from the 6 input parameters for interpolation and extrapolation
interpolation/extrapolation based off input parameter values
ideally train on cheap configurations to predict for expensive configurations
how to simulate extrapolation?

split the data into “inside” and “outside” parameter values and treat outside as extrapolation




my results

random forest interpolation up to 0.99 R2
random forest extrapolation up to 0.94 R2
